title: Schema Design: Keys, Constraints & Normalization
oneLiner: Store each fact once, and make the database itself refuse data that breaks your rules.
keyTakeaway: If the same fact is stored in two places, eventually the two copies will disagree. Normalize so each fact has one home, link tables with foreign keys, and declare your rules (PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK) in the schema (the definition of the tables, their columns and rules) -- the database enforces them for every app and every script, including the ones that forgot to check.
explanation:
A spreadsheet-style table with one row per order and the customer's name and email copied onto each row is easy to start with. The trouble starts when something changes. Ava updates her email, someone runs an UPDATE against the order they were looking at, and now Ava has two emails depending on which order you read. That's an update anomaly, and it's a design problem, not a coding mistake: the design allowed the copies to disagree.

Normalization means splitting data so each fact is stored exactly once. Customers go in a customers table, orders in an orders table, and each order holds a customer_id that points at its customer -- a foreign key. Now there is one row to update, and every order sees the change through a JOIN (see SQL Joins). The usual rule of thumb: every non-key column should describe the key of its own table, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

Constraints are rules the database enforces on every write. PRIMARY KEY: one unique id per row. UNIQUE: no two rows share a value (one account per email). NOT NULL: a value is required. FOREIGN KEY: a reference must point at a row that exists, and that row can't be deleted out from under it. CHECK: any true/false rule on the row, like qty > 0. Validation in the app is still good for friendly error messages, but only the database sees every write -- the import script, the admin tool, the bug in next month's release.

Normalizing isn't always the end state. Reporting databases sometimes copy data on purpose (denormalize) so big reads need fewer joins. That's a deliberate trade made later, for speed, with a plan for keeping copies in sync -- not the default.
